frames.caption_text: Dispatch brings calls, apparatus, personnel, a map, and reference
notes into one workspace.
This lesson follows a read-only reference check in a fictional training department.
From Home, open the menu in the upper-left corner.
Map, POIs, Protocols, and Contacts lead to different kinds of information.
Choose the reference that answers your question before changing
a call or assigning resources.
We will use the map and site records without making a dispatch.
Open Map for a larger view of the Chicago training area.
The folder control in the lower-left corner opens
Map Layers. Academy Staging is enabled in this example.
Choose Hide All and inspect
the changed layer switch, then close
the panel to compare the map.
The blue staging point disappears while the other incident
and unit markers remain.
Reopen the panel and
choose Show All to restore the layer.
These controls change what this map displays; they do not delete
the point or dispatch a resource.
For a named reference, choose POIs from the menu.
The list starts with All types and Name, A to Z.
Select Academy Staging in the type selector, then
enter Staging in Search POIs.
The existing Academy Staging Point remains in the result.
A type filter and a search work together, so check both when a point seems missing.
This example has only one point; it does not demonstrate a change in sorting order.
Read the card before using its location.
It identifies Academy Staging Point, its Academy Staging type, a Destination badge,
and a clearly marked training address.
The note calls it a fictional exercise assembly point and says it provides
no real deployment or access approval.
Use those stored details to confirm you found the intended reference.
A point on this map is not evidence that a device reported its position
or that a crew reached the site.
Protocols is a separate menu entry for departmental procedures.
Here the page says No protocols found and explains that none have
been created for the department. That is the available information for this exercise.
There is no procedure to open or follow in this recording.
Treat an empty reference page as something to resolve through your authorized
departmental process, rather than assuming the app supplied the missing instructions.
Open Contacts to find the site record.
Enter Warehouse in Search contacts, then
open Training Warehouse, marked fictional.
Contact Details keeps that name and the Company category above its reference tabs.
The Contact Information section shows an email address and office
phone for this training record.
Confirm the identity before reading further; a similar
place name is not enough.
We inspect the stored reference here without calling, emailing, opening an
address link, or changing the contact.
The supporting tabs stay with the same contact.
Open Notes: this
warehouse has no notes in that tab.
required_labels: No notes found for this contact

frames.caption_text: Pre-Plan explicitly
says that no pre-incident plan has been recorded. Files says
required_labels: No pre-incident plan has been recorded for this contact.

frames.caption_text: that no files have been attached.
required_labels: No files have been attached to this contact.

frames.caption_text: Check each message rather than assuming a tab contains material
because its name is present.
Calls opens
Related calls, covering calls linked to this contact and
calls at its linked occupancies.
The example returns No related calls.
That result describes this contact query; it does not mean the dispatch
console has no active incidents.
Settings is lower in the menu.
App Info identifies the app, version, and environment, which
helps when requesting support.
Scrolling reveals Preferences, including Theme, Language, and Keep
Alive, followed by Support links.
We leave those settings and links unchanged; this browser view
does not prove a device wake lock or native hardware behavior.
Apply the same map, point, and contact checks to fire and EMS,
community-care or mental-health teams, search and rescue, security, wildland
contractors, and industrial teams.
The common task is finding the right place and recognizing which reference
information is actually available.
